## Data & Analytical Question

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="58%"}

#### Research question

Can information recorded during an **emergency department visit** help
distinguish different patient disposition outcomes?

```{.r}

        Patient     Triage      Clinical      Care       Hospital
           │           │           │           │            │
      demographics   acuity     vitals      meds /       hospital
                     arrival    diagnosis   procedures    features

```

:::

::: {.column width="42%"}

From U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC)

:::

## Understanding the Outcome

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="53%"}

#### 16 non-mutually-exclusive indicators

![](data/img/disposition-prevalence.png){width=100% fig-alt="Prevalence of the original NHAMCS emergency department disposition indicators"}

:::

::: {.column width="47%"}

#### Overlap was structured

![](data/img/disposition-combinations.png){width=100% fig-alt="Most frequent combinations of NHAMCS emergency department disposition indicators"}

:::

:::

<div class="flow">

<div class="flow-step">

<strong>16 binary indicators</strong>

<small>Yes / No<br>Non-mutually-exclusive</small>

</div>

<div class="flow-arrow">→</div>

<div class="flow-step">

<strong>Resolve overlaps</strong>

<small>Predefined priority rule<br>select one disposition</small>

</div>

<div class="flow-arrow">→</div>

<div class="flow-step">

<strong>Restrict analytic scope</strong>

<small>Exclude death / DOA, other,<br>no answer, and follow-up</small>

</div>

<div class="flow-arrow">→</div>

<div class="flow-step accent">

<strong>11 labels → 5 classes</strong>

<small>6,757 visits<br>mutually exclusive target</small>

</div>

</div>

<div class="method-note">

<strong>Modeling decision:</strong> This target definition was an analytical simplification for the course project, not a clinically validated disposition hierarchy.

</div>


## Model Performance & Error Analysis

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="43%"}

### Comparing four model families

![](data/img/model-comparison.png){width=100%}

**XGBoost** achieved the highest accuracy and F1, while **SVM** had the highest reported AUC.

:::

::: {.column width="57%"}

### Random Forest: where did errors occur?

![](data/img/rf-confusion-normalized.png){width=100%}

**Transfer** was frequently classified as admit; **left early** was also harder to distinguish than admit or returned.


:::

:::

**Takeaway:** Aggregate performance was only part of the evaluation—class-specific errors revealed substantial differences in how well the five outcomes could be distinguished.


## What Did the Model Learn?

::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="55%"}

### Random Forest feature importance

![](data/img/rf-feature-importance.png)

<div class="model-summary">

**Length of visit and medication utilization were among the strongest
predictors**, alongside vital signs, procedures, and hospital characteristics.

</div>

:::

::: {.column width="45%"}

### From course project to healthcare research

<div class="reflection-item">

<span class="reflection-number">01</span>

<div>
<strong>Prediction timing matters</strong>

Some highly ranked variables—such as length of visit and medications—accumulate
during the ED visit and may not be available at initial triage.
</div>

</div>

<div class="reflection-item">

<span class="reflection-number">02</span>

<div>
<strong>Outcome definition matters</strong>

Raw NHAMCS disposition indicators overlap and can represent different parts
of the patient's care trajectory.
</div>

</div>

<div class="reflection-item">

<span class="reflection-number">03</span>

<div>
<strong>How I would extend the study</strong>

Define the prediction time point and outcome with clinical collaborators,
then restrict predictors accordingly and evaluate calibration and uncertainty.
</div>

</div>

:::

:::

<div class="takeaway">

**Reflection:** The project is best interpreted as retrospective classification
of observed ED outcomes—not evidence of triage-time predictive performance.

</div>
